```{r vignette-options, include = FALSE}
source("../_setup.R", local = TRUE)
```

This page answers questions that come up when using mostr, including the
error messages that users run into most often. The examples use a small
simulated trial, in the same form as in [the get-started vignette](mostr.html): eight states of
the ACTT-2 scale, of which state 8 (death) is absorbing.

```{r setup}
library(mostr)

trial <- sim_markov("actt2", n_patients = 150, follow_up_time = 14, seed = 1)
model_data <- prepare_markov_data(trial, absorbing_state = 8)
fit <- mostm(y ~ yprev + time + tx, data = model_data, id_var = "id")
```

## Getting started

### Which function do I need?

`?mostr` lists every function by what you want to do: fit a model, estimate
state occupancy probabilities (SOPs) or time in states, compare treatments,
add confidence intervals, simulate data, plot, and check the model.
[The get-started vignette](mostr.html) runs through a complete analysis.

### Can I use a model that I fitted with `rms::orm()`, `VGAM::vglm()`, or `rmsb::blrm()`?

No. Fit the model with `mostm()` instead, and choose the package with
`engine = "orm"`, `"vglm"`, or `"blrm"`. `mostm()` stores each patient's
starting row and the data the other functions need, which a model fitted
directly lacks. Supplying `newdata` does not help:

```{r direct-fit, error = TRUE}
direct <- rms::orm(y ~ yprev + time + tx, data = model_data, x = TRUE, y = TRUE)
avg_sops(direct, newdata = model_data[model_data$time == 1, ], times = 1:14, absorb = "8")
```

Arguments of the engine's own fitting function can be passed to `mostm()`,
for example `maxit` for `rms::orm()` or `family` and `constraints` for
`VGAM::vglm()`; see `?mostm`.

### Do I need an rms `datadist`?

No. mostr does not use one. Set one with `options(datadist = ...)` only if
you also want rms's own summaries of an `"orm"` fit, such as
`summary(fit)`.

### Why does `mostm()` refuse `factor()` in the formula?

For the `"orm"` and `"blrm"` engines, categorical predictors must be factor
or character columns of the data, because mostr rebuilds the model's design
for new visits and patients from those columns:

```{r factor-formula, error = TRUE}
mostm(y ~ factor(yprev) + time + tx, data = model_data, id_var = "id")
```

Create the factor as a column, as `prepare_markov_data()` does for `yprev`,
and use the column in the formula.

## Estimating probabilities and times

### Why are my probabilities for days 7, 14 and 28 not the probabilities on those days?

SOPs are calculated one visit after another: the first value of `times` is
the first transition from the starting state, and each further value is one
more transition. With daily visits, `times = c(1, 7, 14)` gives the
probabilities after 1, 2 and 3 transitions, labelled 1, 7 and 14. mostr warns
about this:

```{r skipped-times, warning = TRUE}
probabilities <- avg_sops(fit, times = c(1, 7, 14), absorb = "8")
```

Request every visit, such as `times = 1:14`, and keep the rows you need. If
your visits are scheduled at uneven intervals, see
[the article on time as a factor](factor-time-orm-sops.html).

### What does the error about "state level(s) not represented in the fitted transition data" mean?

Usually that `absorb` is missing. `prepare_markov_data()` removed the rows
after death, so the model never sees a transition out of state 8 and cannot
predict one. Name the absorbing states in `absorb`, and mostr keeps the
probability of being in them instead of predicting transitions out of them:

```{r missing-absorb, error = TRUE}
avg_sops(fit, times = 1:14)
```

```{r with-absorb}
probabilities <- avg_sops(fit, times = 1:14, absorb = "8")
```

### Why does `newdata` with a patient in an absorbing state give an error?

A patient who has died cannot move to another state, so there is nothing to
predict. Each profile in `newdata` must start outside the states in `absorb`;
remove the others from `newdata` first.

### Do I need to supply `y_levels`?

Usually not. If `y_levels` is `NULL`, mostr reads the states from the fitted
model. If you supply it, give one entry per state, in the order the model
uses; a vector with the wrong number of states gives an error that states
both numbers.

### How do I get the expected time in a state instead of probabilities?

Use `avg_state_time()` for the expected number of days in each state, or in a
group of states given by `state_sets`, and `avg_comparisons()` with
`estimand = "time_in_state"` to compare treatments. The time is the sum of the
SOPs over the requested days, so over `times = 1:14` the times of all states
add up to 14 days:

```{r state-time}
days <- avg_state_time(
  fit,
  variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
  state_sets = list(outside_hospital = c("1", "2")),
  times = 1:14,
  absorb = "8"
)
days
```

For visits that are not daily, `time_map` gives the elapsed time of each
visit; see [the article on time as a factor](factor-time-orm-sops.html).

### How do I estimate effects within subgroups?

Pass the grouping column to `by` in `avg_sops()`, `avg_state_time()` or
`avg_comparisons()`, for example `by = "sex"`. Each group's estimate is the
average over that group's patients. Analytical confidence intervals are not
yet available with `by`; use `method = "mvn"` or `method = "fwb"` in
`inferences()`. [The fractional weighted bootstrap article](fractional-weighted-bootstrap-sops.html) shows an
example.

## Confidence intervals

### Which method should I use in `inferences()`?

| `method` | What it does | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `"delta"` | Calculates intervals from formulas, without random draws | First-order, full proportional-odds models from the `"orm"` or `"vglm"` engine |
| `"mvn"` (default) | Draws coefficients from a multivariate normal distribution and recalculates the results for each draw | Any frequentist model |
| `"bootstrap"` | Refits the model to patients resampled with replacement | Averages from `avg_sops()`, `avg_state_time()` and `avg_comparisons()` |
| `"fwb"` | Refits the model with a random positive weight for each patient | Averages, and results for each patient |

`"delta"` is the fastest and gives the same answer every time.
[The analytical confidence intervals article](analytical-confidence-intervals.html) explains it, and
[the article comparing MVN simulation and the bootstrap](mvn-vs-bootstrap-orm-sops.html) compares the other methods. Models
fitted with `engine = "blrm"` already carry posterior intervals, so
`inferences()` is not needed for them.

### Why does `inferences(method = "delta")` stop with an error?

The analytical method does not yet cover every model and result. It stops
with an error, rather than giving a different kind of interval, for

- partial proportional-odds models and second-order models;
- ratios (`comparison = "ratio"`) and `estimand = "time_benefit"`;
- results averaged within groups (`by`); and
- Bayesian models from `engine = "blrm"`.

For these, use `method = "mvn"`, `"bootstrap"` or `"fwb"`.

### Should I use conditional or unconditional variance?

Both are chosen through `vcov` in `inferences(method = "delta")` and give the
same estimates with different intervals.

- **Conditional variance** (`vcov = "conditional"`) accounts for the
  uncertainty in the estimated model coefficients, and treats the patients'
  starting states and covariates as given. It describes the average for these
  particular patients.
- **Unconditional variance** (`vcov = "unconditional"`) also accounts for
  which patients happened to be sampled, and for their role in estimating the
  coefficients. It describes the average in the population the patients come
  from. It is the default for averages.

Results for each patient, from `sops()`, `state_time()` and `comparisons()`,
support only conditional variance, because they do not average over sampled
patients.

### Why is unconditional variance not available for my results?

Unconditional variance needs the patients stored with the fit, so it is not
available when you average over your own `newdata`:

```{r newdata-unconditional, error = TRUE}
starting_rows <- model_data[model_data$time == 1, ]
avg_sops(fit, newdata = starting_rows, variables = list(tx = c(0, 1)),
         times = 1:14, absorb = "8") |>
  inferences(method = "delta")
```

It is also not available for fits with `weights`, for penalized `"orm"` fits,
or when `variables` sets the previous state (for example
`variables = list(yprev = c("4", "5"))`). In all these cases pass
`vcov = "conditional"`.

### Why are the standard error and confidence interval `NA`?

There are two common reasons.

- You compared a variable that the model does not use. Setting it cannot
  change any prediction, so the difference is exactly 0 (or the ratio exactly
  1) and has no uncertainty. Check the spelling of the variable in
  `variables` and in the model formula.
- An estimated probability is exactly 0 or 1, for example after rounding. The
  analytical intervals for probabilities are formed on the log-odds scale,
  which is undefined at 0 and 1, so those limits are `NA` and `inferences()`
  warns. `conf_type = "wald"` gives limits from the estimate plus or minus a
  multiple of the standard error instead.

### Why do my simulation or bootstrap intervals change every time?

They are based on random draws. Pass `seed` to `inferences()` to get the same
draws, and the same intervals, every time. Increasing `n_draws` makes the
intervals less variable from run to run.

### Why does the ordinary bootstrap stop with an error?

A resample drawn with replacement can leave out every patient who was ever in
a rare state, or every patient of a small group in `by`. The model refitted to
that resample cannot predict for those states or groups, so
`inferences(method = "bootstrap")` stops and says why. For the same reason,
it is not available for results for each patient from `sops()`,
`state_time()` and `comparisons()`. Use
`method = "fwb"`, which keeps every patient in every refit.

### How can I use the draws for my own summaries?

`inferences()` stores the simulation or bootstrap draws by default
(`return_draws = TRUE`). `get_draws()` returns them as a data frame with one
row per draw and estimate; the `draw` column holds the value in that draw.

### How do I get the covariance between two estimates?

After `inferences(method = "delta")`, `vcov()` returns the covariance matrix
of the estimates; the square roots of its diagonal are the standard errors.
The matrix has one row and column per estimate, so it can be large. Pass
`rows` to request only the estimates you need:

```{r vcov}
probabilities_ci <- inferences(probabilities, method = "delta")
covariance <- vcov(probabilities_ci, rows = 1:3)
unname(sqrt(diag(covariance)))
probabilities_ci$std.error[1:3]
```

The option `mostr.delta_max_bytes` caps the memory that these calculations
may use. `vcov()` is not available after simulation or bootstrap; use
`get_draws()` instead.

### How can I make the bootstrap faster?

Pass `workers` to `inferences()`, or to `bootstrap_model_coefs()`, to refit
the model in several R processes at once. With `engine = "vglm"`,
`use_coefstart = TRUE` starts each refit from the original coefficients,
which can shorten the fitting.

## Fitting problems

### `mostm()` says the covariance of the coefficients cannot be computed

This happens when the fitting algorithm has not converged, or when some
coefficients grow without bound because a transition never occurs in the
data, for example from a rare state to death. For the `"orm"` engine,
the arguments `opt_method = "LM"`, `scale = TRUE` and a larger `maxit`, which
are passed on to `rms::orm()`, often help it converge. If a transition never
occurs, simplify the model, for example by combining rare states.

### What do `weights` in `mostm()` change?

The weights are used only to fit the model. mostr's bootstrap keeps each
row's weight when it resamples patients, and the fractional weighted bootstrap
multiplies each row's weight by its patient's random weight. `avg_sops()` and
the other averaging functions give every patient the same weight, and
`inferences(method = "delta")` offers only conditional variance for a weighted
fit.

### How do I check that the model describes the data?

Draw the same summary from the observed trajectories and from the fitted
model, and compare them. `plot_transitions()`, `plot_correlation()` and
`plot_variogram()` accept either the observed trajectories or a fit from
`mostm()`, and `plot_sops()` accepts either the observed trajectories or the
result of `avg_sops()`; see [the proportional-odds article](full-po-sops.html). If the observed correlations between days fall
off more slowly than the model's, a second-order model
([the second-order article](second-order-orm-sops.html)) may fit better. If effects seem to
differ between states, see [the partial proportional-odds article](partial-po-vglm-sops.html).
